 Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other
 matter within its jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal Code.
 If you wish to address City Council, please complete the card that is provided at the rear entrance to Council Chambers
 and hand the card to the Sergeant at Arms. City Council will hear public comment on items listed on the agenda during
 discussion of the matter and prior to a vote. City Council will hear public comment on matters not listed on the agenda
 during the Oral Communications period.

 Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless
 certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain
 matters for consideration at a future City Council meeting.

 Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council:
  ♦ Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less.
  ♦ Comments should be directed to the City Council as a whole and not directed to individual Councilmembers.

 Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City
 meeting or other services offered by this City, please contact the City Clerk’s department, (562) 929-5720. Assisted
 listening devices are available at this meeting. Ask the City Clerk if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda
 and documents in the agenda packet can be made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability.
 Notification of at least 48 hours prior to the meeting or time when services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring
 that reasonable arrangements can be made to provide accessibility to the meeting or service.

 posted will also be made available for public inspection.

  REGULAR MEETING

Mayor Rios called the meeting to order at 6:12 p.m. in the Council Chambers, Norwalk
City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Responding to roll call were
Councilmembers Perez, Ramirez, and Valencia, and Mayor Rios. Vice Mayor Ayala was
absent. Also present were Jesus M. Gomez, City Manager; Arnold M. Alvarez, City
Attorney; and Theresa Devoy, City Clerk.

The invocation was delivered by Pastor Myrna Brito, Spirit Life Community Church,
followed by the flag salute, led by Dominic Ortiz Olivas, Earl E. Edmondson Elementary
School.

CLOSED SESSION REPORT

The City Attorney indicated there was no reportable action taken on the matters discussed
in closed session.

CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

City Council thanked Public Safety, Emergency Operations Center, Social Services,
Public Services, Communication and Public Affairs, the Los Angeles Sheriffs, and the Los
Angeles County Fire Departments for all their hard work keeping residents safe and
informed during the recent storms. Councilmember Perez shared that City newsletters
were distributed and urged residents to review them for important information and
programming; and requested the meeting be adjourned in memory of Lou Banas, former
City Council Member and Mayor. Councilmember Ramirez shared that employee David
Plaza, Community Worker, was recognized by Little Lake School District for his
contributions in helping our youth; highlighted the start of the Youth Intervention
Academy; congratulated former employee Erika Pena for graduating from the Fire
Academy; announced that Lions Club International is hosting a speech contest February
7 in Council Chambers; and invited all to attend the Norwalk Lions Club Pancake
Breakfast at the Norwalk Arts and Sports Complex February 11. Councilmember
Valencia reported on her attendance at the Third-Gen Nursing Academy Grand Opening
and the Southeast Water Coalition Board of Directors meeting where she announced the
city will host the meetings. Mayor Rios shared that she was part of a public service
announcement made for the Gaining Early Awareness and Readiness for Undergraduate
Program; reported on her attendance at the Santa Sleigh Appreciation dinner, Angel Tree
Appreciation event, Greater Los Angeles Homeless Count, Youth Sports and Fitness
Exposition, and thanked all who volunteered for the various events; participated in the

Background:

Norwalk Transit System (NTS) issued a Request for Proposal (RFP) No. 24-731 for a
professional services agreement for Project Management, Design Services, Construction
Management, and Inspection Services for NTS’s Bus Stop Equity Project (BSEP) for
improvement to bus stops within the City. The purpose of the BSEP is to modernize and upgrade
the bus stops to alleviate the harmful climate impacts on NTS’s patrons by installing amenities
that will protect patrons from the intense heat and wet weather.

Four proposals were received from the following firms: (1) Onward Engineering (Onward), (2)
MARRS Services, Inc. (MARRS), (3) PSOMAS, and (4) Virginkar & Associates, Inc. (Virginkar).
Virginkar’s proposal was rejected based on failure to follow instructions from the RFP as it relates
to the cost proposals not being submitted separately.

NTS staff evaluated the remaining three proposals in keeping with the following RFP
requirement criteria: qualifications, related experience, proposed project team, detailed work
plan and completeness of responses. This resulted in the following ranking of the proposals:

  Firm  Total Score
 1  Onward Engineering  94%
 2  PSOMAS  92%
 3  MARRS Services  92%

After the initial ranking, each firm was interviewed by NTS staff to obtain additional feedback as
it relates to overall experience with managing a BSEP including project management to
construction management, design criteria, proposed team, and regulatory compliance. This
resulted in the following overall ranking of the proposers:

  Firm  Total Score
 1  Onward Engineering  97%

Onward’s total cost proposal of $500,660 for the BSEP was determined to be fair and reasonable
in keeping with prevailing labor rates and wages. Onward will be managing the project from
design phase to installation of the bus stop shelters and amenities.

Fiscal Impact:

The total project estimated cost of $500,660 will be will be funded through the use of Transit
Reserves. These funds are included in the Fiscal Year 2023/24 Transportation Department
capital budget and there is no impact to the general fund.

assisted) at the Bloomfield Sewer Lift Station.

epoxy coating of corroded force mains at both locations, the contractor was unable to complete
that work. Work not completed under Project No. 7520 will be done as a separate future
project. The remaining scope of work for the sewer lift stations and manholes was completed
on December 13, 2023. Total revised construction costs, including staff time is $307,486, which

SUBJECT:  PUBLIC HEARING - RESOLUTION NO. 24-11 – APPLICATION FOR GRANT
  FUNDING FOR A PERMANENT LOCAL HOUSING ALLOCATION PROGRAM

Background:

In 2017, Governor Brown signed a 15-bill housing package aimed at addressing the State’s
housing shortage and high housing costs. This included Senate Bill 2, known as the Building
Homes and Jobs Act (Act) that became effective in January 2018, establishing a $75 recording
fee on real estate documents to increase the supply of affordable housing. The Act establishes
the Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) program, administered by the California
Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD). The PLHA provides a permanent
source of funding to cities and counties to help meet the unmet need for affordable housing and
increase the supply of affordable housing units.

In December 2023, the HCD announced the release of the 2023 PLHA Notice of Funding
Availability (NOFA) for approximately $296 million. Funding is provided through formula grants
to entitlement jurisdictions based on the formula prescribed under federal law for the Community
Development Block Grant (CDBG) program over a five-year funding period. The City is an
entitlement jurisdiction, and is eligible to receive an estimated $3,556,572 over the five-year
funding period. The annual PLHA amounts are subject to change as funding is generated
through a fee on real estate transactions, which may fluctuate from year to year.

Five-Year PLHA Plan

To access the funds, the City must submit a five-year plan (plan) that will describe how funds
will be allocated for the selected eligible activity; additional threshold requirements must be met
for first-time applicants as detailed in the application (Attachment No. 2). Staff reviewed the list
of eligible activities and propose the use of grant funds for:
 City Council  February 20, 2024
Resolution No. 24-11 – Application for PLHA Program  Page No. 2

“§301(a)(2) The predevelopment, development, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of
Affordable rental and ownership housing, including Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), that meets
the needs of a growing workforce earning up to 120 percent pof Area Median Income (AMI), or
150 percent of AMI in High-cost areas. ADUs shall be available for occupancy for a term of no
less than 30 days.”

Specifically, the City will contract with a qualified consultant through the Request for Proposals
process to develop a Permit-Ready ADU program. The consultant activities may include, but are
not limited to: compiling local data/inventory, conducting outreach to confirm ADU needs,
develop policies, prepare pre-approved concept designs and full build designs, and prepare ADU
guidelines. The intended use of PLHA funds is consistent with the City’s Certified Housing
Element, Program 1.4 Affordable Housing Development Assistance that allows the City to
provide incentives to residents to encourage the development of ADUs to facilitate housing
production and affordability goals set forth in the 2013-2021 Regional Housing Needs Allocation.

PLHA applications must be submitted by February 29, 2024.

Fiscal Impact:

Staff expects the City will receive a total of $3,556,572 over the five-year funding period and is
not required to provide any matching funds. There is no impact to the general fund.

SUBJECT:  HEART OF NORWALK SPECIFIC PLAN UPDATE

Background:

On July 6, 2021, the City Council adopted The Heart of Norwalk Vision Plan for the future of San
Antonio Village and the Firestone Corridor, two key neighborhoods in the center of the City. The
Plan was developed in partnership with the City, the Southern California Association of
Governments (SCAG) and the consulting firm, The Arroyo Group (TAG). This Vision Plan sets
the overall tone for how the study area can grow in both the commercial and housing sectors,
while balancing place making and open spaces. The Vision Plan emphasizes providing new
commercial amenities, open spaces, complete streets, and affordable housing to support
Norwalk residents. In order to implement this vision, staff initiated the development of a Specific
Plan that will establish zoning regulations and development standards to make this vision into a
reality.

Discussion

The proposed Specific Plan effort intends to establish zoning regulations that will permit housing
and desired commercial uses while ensuring that each development contributes to community
goals. It will also establish a program of street, open space, and infrastructure projects to support
the vision of the plan and future growth, and propose funding and implementation measures
needed to implement the proposed Specific Plan.

The Heart of Norwalk project area contains a wide variety of commercial and residential zoning
districts. Staff notes that currently within the commercially zoned properties, housing is permitted
with a Conditional Use Permit. It is estimated that these commercial sites could reasonably be
developed with 2,053 residential units under current zoning regulations. The Specific Plan is
intended to be implemented over a 30-year period.
 City Council  February 20, 2024
Heart of Norwalk Specific Plan Update  Page No. 2

Additionally, the development of the Specific Plan will help the City accomplish its Regional
Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) of 5,034 units. The Housing Element accounted many of the
sites within the Heart of Norwalk area as residential inventory sites available for development.
Therefore, the Housing Element contains a program that commits to adopting the Heart of
Norwalk Specific Plan, which would allow residential use.

Community Feedback

The project team have received robust and consistent input for the project since the beginning
of the Vision Plan process in fall 2020. The Vision Plan outreach campaign engaged
approximately 5,300 residents between December 2020 and March 2021. Nearly 100 residents
attended four online events that were held in February and March 2021, 363 surveys were
completed by community members, and over 3,000 residents engaged with Heart of Norwalk
social media content.

Outreach in the Specific Plan process has consisted of virtual and in-person community
workshops and participation at three Front Street events in the summer of 2022. Further
community workshops and social media engagement will take place prior to the adoption of the
Specific Plan.

Throughout the outreach process, members of the public have consistently expressed the desire
for high-quality local commercial options, places to enjoy in groups and spend time in public.
They desire an authentic center to the City, with local and national businesses, places to walk
and spend time, nightlife, and spaces that can encourage and celebrate local culture, such as
performance arts spaces.

Front Street has been identified as a focal area for local business and nightlife, preserving older
buildings and the historic feel of the street, and possibly catering to the younger population of
the community. Norwalk Town Square, on the other hand, is seen as a place with shopping,
family entertainment, and easy parking. Multifamily residential uses were supported as an
appropriate part of these districts, especially as they help make the desired commercial
amenities possible. Finally, through surveys and workshops, members of the public also
expressed a desire to connect these districts through streets that prioritize walking, biking and
public space over traffic movement.

Specific Plan Progress

The project team has initiated the development of the Specific Plan and the Environmental
Impact Report (EIR). As part of this process, the City will continue to receive public feedback
and additional input regarding the proposed land use plan in order to continue the preparation
of the Specific Plan’s zoning regulations and EIR. Additionally, the project team has developed
renderings to help envision the potential of the different districts within the Heart of Norwalk.
 City Council  February 20, 2024
Heart of Norwalk Specific Plan Update  Page No. 3

Next Steps

Once a land use plan of the Heart of Norwalk has been established. The project team will
continue with the preparation of the Specific Plan and the environmental analysis for the project.
The Specific Plan is anticipated for consideration before the City Council in winter 2024.

Background:

Enclosed are mid-year budget projections for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2023/24 Budget. The
projections and recommended budget adjustments are based upon the final Audited Financial
Statements for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023 and six months actual expenses and
revenues during the current fiscal year.

General Fund:

FY 2022/23

Based on audited results, net of accounting Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB)
adjustments; all revenues, except sales and real property transfer taxes outperformed the City’s
revenue estimates. In addition to ongoing revenue sources, the City received $2.6 million in
one-time revenues from a legal settlement and energy rebates. The total revenue collected
amounted to $78 million, 9% or $6.1 million over the budgetary estimates. Expenditures were
$7.6 million, 9% under the budget, due mainly to savings realized under: Personnel ($4.5
million), Sheriff’s Contract ($1.8 million) and other expenditures ($1.3 million).

The outcome of the above mentioned positive financial impacts result is the General Fund ending
available balance of $28.1 million, which is $2.4 million higher than anticipated during the
preparation of the FY 2023/24 Budget.
 City Council  February 20, 2024
Resolution No. 24-10 Budget FY 2023/24  Page No. 2

Attachment No. 1 provides an overview of the City’s financial results for the fiscal year ending
June 30, 2023.

FY 2023/24

The current FY 2023/24 budget year-to-date results indicate that the City is on target with the
projections, with the exception of the following:

Revenue Adjustments:

For FY 2023/24, the overall General Fund revenues are expected to outperform the original
revenue estimates by a total of $2.1 million, or 2.9%, and reach $77.1 million. As in the prior
fiscal year, this year’s revenues include the last allocation of $2.9 million from the American
Rescue Plan Act’s (ARPA) Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Fund (SLFRF) that
provides financial relief to the General Fund for loss of revenues during the pandemic. The
proposed increase of $2.1 million in General Fund revenues estimates is a combination of the
following revisions:

Sales Taxes – Local Tax & Measure P: The City’s largest revenue category is slightly under the
anticipated revenues. Current year revenues are expected to remain flat when compared to the
prior year’s actual revenue amount of $26.2 million, exceeding it only by $123 thousand. Staff
recommends decreasing the current estimates by $52 thousand, to a combined total of $26.3
million. This negative adjustment results reflects the state of economy and is in line with regional
economy trends.

Property value derived revenues represent the second most significant portion of General Fund
revenues. Projections for all categories combined are proposed to be increased by $1
million. The detail of adjustments is as follows:

  •  Property Tax In Lieu of VLF: This category is estimated to increase substantially from the
  original FY 2023/24 projections. The City receives two equal allocations from the State in
  January and May. Based on the amount received in January, staff estimates this revenue
  will be $639 thousand higher than projected.

  •  No/Low and South-East Recreational Park Property Tax: Based on the year-to-date
  receipts, staff recommends increasing these categories by $215 thousand and $75
  thousand, respectively.

  •  Property Tax allocated to the City from Successors of the former Redevelopment
  Agencies is estimated to reach $920 thousand, which is $70 thousand higher than staff’s
  original estimates.

Utility User Tax (UUT): As the prices of electricity and gas continue to increase, so do the City’s
UUT revenues. Staff estimates that this year the UUT will generate $6 million in revenues, $389
thousand over the original budget estimates.
 City Council  February 20, 2024

Transient Occupancy Tax: Year to date receipts from local hotels are trending to reach $1.7
million, which is $80 thousand higher than our original estimates.

Franchise Fees: The annual revenues are estimated to be $388 thousand over the budgeted
amount, primarily under trash, electricity and gas categories. However, Cable TV franchises
continue declining from year to year, as the streaming services become more prevalent.

Real Property Transfer Tax: Receipts are lagging projections by $10 thousand, as sales of single
family homes are declining primarily due to the high interest rates.

Other General Fund revenues will increase by a net amount of $353 thousand, out of which
approximately $187 thousand will be generated by Recreation fees for services. Details of
revenue budget revisions can be found in Exhibit A attached to Resolution No. 24-10.

Expenditure Adjustments:

The proposed mid-year budget revisions increase the operational spending by $1.2 million, out
of which about $108 thousand is under personnel cost; $929 thousand is under other operating
expenses; and the remainder, $115 thousand, is requested for minor capital outlay
purchases. The most significant changes are as follows:

  •  Communications/Public Affairs, Multimedia, Social Services and Recreation personnel
  changes represent about $108 thousand in additional personnel cost for the remainder of
  the fiscal year. The requested personnel changes are detailed in Exhibit C to Resolution
  No. 24-10.

  •  Under operations and maintenance, net $929 thousand budget increase is requested to
  cover various departmental needs. Among the most significant requests are: $185
  thousand to fund various contractual services city-wide; $169 thousand for computer
  software and support costs; $161 thousand under vehicle maintenance costs, which
  includes a request of $50 thousand to refurbish the City’s mobile command center unit.

  •  Additional appropriations to cover the minor capital outlays total $115 thousand.

Proposed revisions to the General Fund expenditure budget are detailed in Exhibit B attached
to Resolution No. 24-10.

In addition, the City’s capital reserves for street repairs are proposed to be replenished by $3
million.

Taking into consideration the proposed budget revisions, the estimated unassigned General
Fund balance will be approximately $15.2 million, which is 1% ($580 thousand) above the City’s
reserve policy, currently set at 20% of operating and minor capital outlays budget. Exhibit D to
Resolution No. 24-10 provides more detail of the General Fund balance projections.

Park Renovation Fund: The existing budget includes $1.9 million for the sports lighting project

Street Renovation Fund: Staff is requesting a total of $5.5 million to secure funding for the

Transportation: Staff proposes an increase of $0.6 million in operating revenues and a $0.4

Water: Operating revenue estimates can be increased by $0.7 million and expenses are
